name: Rubber Stamp
basis: why: one flat colour or nothing, with uneven pressure and wear; how: threshold, ink-loss noise, pinholes, tilt, multiply onto paper

lumenary.blurb: Your picture as a hand-inked rubber stamp pressed a little crooked on paper: patchy ink, a border and a stamped word.

facts.bestOn: High contrast pictures and bold silhouettes

why: A rubber stamp prints one flat colour or nothing, so the picture is cut to black and white and the interest comes from imperfection: uneven pressure, worn patches, pinholes and a slightly crooked angle. Those flaws are what make a stamp look pressed by a person.
how: Cut the picture to black and white at the chosen threshold, after a small random wobble so the edge is ragged.
Add a double border and a banner with the word cut out of it on the same plate.
Remove ink with a slow noise for uneven pressure, a mid-scale noise for worn patches, and scattered single-pixel pinholes.
Rotate the inked layer by the tilt angle.
Combine it with the paper by multiplication, as ink soaking into fibres darkens what is beneath.
history: Seals pressed into clay or wax are thousands of years old. The rubber stamp became practical after Charles Goodyear’s vulcanisation of rubber in 1839 and was in common office use by the late nineteenth century, to date, approve and file. Today stamps are a staple of crafts, scrapbooking and printmaking.
terms: Treating rubber with sulphur and heat so that it stays elastic and firm.
A tiny spot where no ink was transferred.
A way of combining layers so that the result is never lighter than either.
paragraphs: A rubber stamp prints one flat colour or nothing, so the picture is cut to black and white: a pixel is inked where its brightness (stretched and blurred a little) is below the “where the ink goes” slider, after adding a small random wobble so the edge is ragged. A double border and a banner with the word, cut out of the banner, are drawn on the same plate.

Inking is never even. Three things remove ink from the plate: a slow noise for uneven pressure (ink strength between about 0.6 and 1), a mid-scale noise whose high values mark worn patches where the ink is almost gone, and a scatter of single-pixel pinholes. All three scale with the worn-rubber slider. The inked layer is then turned about the centre by the tilt angle and combined with the paper by multiplication, as ink soaking into the fibres darkens whatever is beneath it.

equations.note: Where the stamp carries ink; n is smooth noise and r a random number.
Ink opacity: κ is 1 on the plate; χ is 0.1 on worn patches and 0 on pinholes.
Multiply blend of ink and paper.

presets.text: Blue ink with heavy wear looks like a long-used stamp.
A bigger tilt makes it look pressed in a hurry.
